## Why it exists {#why-it-exists}

### The mission {#mission}

Physics by Construction exists so that anyone with an undergraduate
background can learn physics by building it, in the open: writing a model as
a program, testing it against measurements and against independent methods,
and, where it can be done, proving it. It extends the same discipline to the
use of language models and AI agents in science, which are taught as
instruments whose output is checked, not as authorities.

### The educational philosophy {#philosophy}

Physics is best understood by building, experimenting, and verifying results
yourself. A textbook states a result; here you construct it as a program,
test it against measurements or against a second method, and, where it can be
done, prove it. Doing all three on one problem shows what each kind of
evidence can and cannot establish.

A result is not finished when a program prints it. It is finished when you
know what it was checked against and where the check stops, so every lesson
says which kind of evidence stands behind its results. The same holds for an
agent: what it reports is a claim to be checked, never a finding by itself.

### Why open source {#why-open-source}

The code behind every simulation, figure, and proof is openly available for
anyone to explore, reproduce, and improve. The project is freely accessible
without registration or tracking.

## Who it is for {#who-it-is-for}

Readers who have undergraduate physics (classical mechanics, calculus, linear
algebra) and solid programming skills: students who want to see a result
computed rather than asserted, researchers who want to check that it
reproduces, and teachers who want material they can run in class. Lessons
state their prerequisites and link out instead of repeating them. Teaching
with a lesson? The [For educators](educators.qmd) page lists the instructor
packs.

## How the site is built {#how-the-site-is-built}

How a result on this site is checked, and what each kind of claim can and
cannot establish, is explained on
[How we verify the science](verify.qmd), which leads to the
[Evidence map](evidence.qmd). [Run the code](reproduce.qmd) says what to
install to reproduce a lesson on your own computer.

- Equations are MathML. Text, code, equations, and figures are readable with
  JavaScript turned off.
- The site is static files. It has no accounts, sets no cookies, runs no
  analytics, and loads nothing from other websites.

The [rendering check](rendering-check.qmd) page shows sample equations, code,
and a figure produced by the build.

## How to contribute

To correct a mistake, propose a change, suggest a dataset, or propose a lesson,
open an issue from one of the forms. The [Contribute](contribute.qmd) page has
the steps.

## How to cite

The repository has a `CITATION.cff` file in the
[Citation File Format](https://citation-file-format.github.io/). GitHub reads
it and offers "Cite this repository". It names the authors, the project
address, the repository, and the licences. It has no DOI: none exists until
the project has a release policy. A suitable citation is "Physics by
Construction", with a link to the page you used.
